Egypt's governorate names are the deepest stack on the whole map: many
run Ancient Egyptian -> Coptic -> Arabic without a break, so Aswan is
still the Egyptian word for a market and Faiyum is still the Coptic for
the lake. A few Arabic elements repeat:
kafr = village      beni = sons of (a tribe)      bahr = sea/great river
gharb = west        sharq = east                  qibli = southern
So Gharbia and Al Sharqia are simply the western and eastern parts of
the Delta, and Kafr el-Sheikh is 'the sheikh's village'.
damietta: From Ancient Egyptian Tamiat through Coptic Tamiati — the name has survived, barely changed, for over three thousand years.
The Fifth Crusade besieged it for eighteen months and took it in 1219; Francis of Assisi crossed the lines here to meet the sultan.
It is Egypt's furniture capital, and most Egyptian households own something made in its workshops.
kafr-el-sheikh: "The sheikh's village" — kafr is a village, a word that starts dozens of Egyptian place names.
Its Burullus lagoon is one of the Delta's great wetlands and a stop on the migration route between Europe and Africa.
Almost entirely agricultural, growing rice and cotton on the Delta's northern edge.
port-said: Named for Said Pasha, the viceroy who granted the Suez Canal concession — the town was built in 1859 with the canal's northern entrance.
It was a free port for decades, so Egyptians came here to buy imported goods when nowhere else had them.
The Anglo-French invasion of 1956 landed here, and the city's resistance is a national story.
dakahlia: From ad-Daqahliyya, named after a village called Daqahla that no longer matters.
Mansoura, its capital, is where Louis IX of France was captured in 1250 — his crusade ended in a house in this town.
It is one of the most productive farming governorates in the Delta.
gharbia: "The western one" — the western half of the Delta between the two Nile branches.
Mahalla al-Kubra in it is Egypt's textile town, and its mill strikes in 2006–08 fed directly into the 2011 uprising.
Tanta's mulid festival for al-Sayyid al-Badawi draws crowds comparable to the Hajj in size.
alexandria: Founded by and named for Alexander the Great in 331 BC, who laid it out himself and was later buried somewhere in it.
Its library was the largest in the ancient world, and its lighthouse one of the seven wonders; both are gone, the lighthouse toppled by earthquakes.
The city has sunk and the sea risen, so parts of the royal quarter, including possibly Cleopatra's palace, lie under the harbour.
al-sharqia: "The eastern one" — the Delta's eastern governorate, the counterpart of Gharbia.
Bubastis here was the cult city of Bastet, the cat goddess, and its festival was described by Herodotus as the rowdiest in Egypt.
It is Egypt's largest producer of oranges, and the Tenth of Ramadan industrial city in it is one of the country's biggest.
beheira: From buhaira, "lake" — for Lake Mariout and the marshes of the western Delta.
Rashid (Rosetta) is here, where a French soldier found the Rosetta Stone in 1799, the key that unlocked hieroglyphs.
The Nubaria reclamation project turned much of its desert edge into farmland from the 1960s.
ismailia: Named for Khedive Ismail, who ruled while the Suez Canal was dug and who bankrupted Egypt building it and much else.
The city was built for the canal company, which is why it has European villas and wide avenues in the middle of the isthmus.
Lake Timsah in it is a natural lake the canal was routed through, and the Muslim Brotherhood was founded in this town in 1928.
monufia: From an older Egyptian place name, Panouf, meaning something like "the good place".
Two Egyptian presidents, Sadat and Mubarak, were both born in this small governorate.
It has no desert at all: every square metre is Delta farmland, and it is one of the most densely populated rural areas on earth.
north-sinai: Sinai's own name is probably from Sin, a Mesopotamian moon god, or from seneh, the Hebrew for the burning bush.
The coastal road across it was the invasion route between Egypt and Asia for four thousand years, walked by armies in both directions.
Its Bedouin tribes have lived here for centuries and speak a dialect closer to that of the Levant than to Nile Egyptian.
qalyubia: Named after the town of Qalyub, an old Delta settlement just north of Cairo.
The Delta Barrages here, begun in 1843, were the first great modern attempt to control the Nile's flow.
It is effectively Cairo's northern suburb now, with Shubra al-Khayma one of the densest industrial towns in the country.
cairo: Al-Qahira, "the victorious", named in 969 for the planet Mars, which was rising when the Fatimids laid the foundations.
The largest city in Africa and the Arab world, and its Islamic quarter has more medieval monuments than any other city on earth.
Egyptians call it Masr — the same word as the country itself, because for most of history it effectively was.
matrouh: Named for Marsa Matruh, whose harbour was ancient Paraetonium; Cleopatra is said to have swum in a cove there.
Egypt's longest Mediterranean coastline, with water clear enough to look Caribbean.
El Alamein is here, where the 1942 battle turned the desert war; three war cemeteries hold about 12,000 graves.
suez: From an old Egyptian name through Arabic as-Suways; the town existed long before the canal took its name.
The canal opened in 1869, cutting the London–Bombay voyage by about 7,000 km, and about 12% of world trade passes through it.
It has no locks, because the Mediterranean and the Red Sea are at effectively the same level.
faiyum: From Coptic phiom, "the lake" — itself from Ancient Egyptian pa-yom, the sea.
Lake Qarun in it is a remnant of a far larger lake, and the oasis is fed by a channel from the Nile dug in the Middle Kingdom.
Its Fayum mummy portraits, painted on wood in the Roman period, are the most lifelike faces to survive from the ancient world.
beni-suef: "Sons of Suef" — beni marks an Arab tribe, a pattern repeated across Middle Egypt.
Meidum here has a pyramid that partly collapsed, leaving a tower surrounded by its own rubble — evidence of how the shape was worked out.
It is one of the poorest governorates and a major producer of Egypt's cement.
giza: From Arabic al-Jiza, "the side" or "the bank" — the west bank, seen from Cairo.
The Great Pyramid was the tallest building in the world for about 3,800 years, longer than anything else has ever held the record.
The Sphinx beside it is carved from a single ridge of limestone left in the quarry.
south-sinai: The southern half of the same Sinai peninsula, where the mountains are.

St Catherine's monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai has been occupied continuously since 565, the oldest working monastery in the world, and holds the second-largest collection of early manuscripts after the Vatican.
Its reefs at Ras Mohammed and the Blue Hole are among the best dive sites on earth.
minya: From Coptic Tmoone, "the residence" — the name kept through Arabic as al-Minya.
Amarna is here, the capital Akhenaten built in a single reign for his one-god religion and which was abandoned right after his death.
It has the largest Christian population share of any governorate, and is called the bride of Upper Egypt.
asyut: From Ancient Egyptian Zawty through Coptic Siout — "guardian", because it guarded the caravan route.
That route, the Darb al-Arba'in, ran forty days to Darfur and carried slaves and goods for centuries.
Its barrage, built in 1902, still controls irrigation for much of Middle Egypt.
sohag: Named for its capital, whose name is of uncertain origin — possibly from a Berber or early Arabic word.
Abydos here was the cult centre of Osiris and holds the king list that gave Egyptologists their chronology.
The Red and White Monasteries near it are among the oldest Coptic buildings standing, from the fifth century.
luxor: From Arabic al-Uqsur, "the palaces", for the temple ruins the Arabs found; the Greeks had called it Thebes.
It holds about a third of the world's ancient monuments by some counts, and the Valley of the Kings is across the river.
Tutankhamun's tomb was found there in 1922, the only royal tomb discovered nearly intact.
qena: From Ancient Egyptian through Coptic Kene, the name of the town.
Dendera in it has a temple to Hathor whose ceiling zodiac was carved under the Romans and is now in the Louvre.
The Qena bend is where the Nile swings sharply east, the sharpest turn in its whole course.
red-sea: Nobody is sure why it is red: the best theories are a seasonal red algal bloom, the red mountains along it, or an old convention of colour-coding compass directions.
It is one of the saltiest seas in the world, and the only one with no river flowing into it.
Its reefs have some of the highest coral cover on earth and are unusually heat-tolerant, which makes them a research priority as oceans warm.
new-valley: Al-Wadi al-Gadid, a name given in the 1950s to a plan to settle the western oases as a second Nile valley.
The largest governorate in Egypt, about 44% of the country, with well under 1% of its people.
Its Kharga, Dakhla and Farafra oases sit over the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer, one of the largest bodies of fossil water in the world.
aswan: From Ancient Egyptian swenett, "trade" or "market" — the frontier town where Egypt traded with Nubia, and the word survived into Arabic unchanged.
Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth using a well here in about 240 BC, and got within a few per cent.
The High Dam of 1970 ended the Nile flood, created Lake Nasser, and forced Abu Simbel to be cut into blocks and moved uphill.
rashid: Rosetta to Europeans, Rashid in Arabic — the name means "the rightly guided".
The Rosetta Stone was found here in 1799 by a French soldier digging a fort foundation.
Its Greek, demotic and hieroglyphic text let Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.
dumyat: The Arabic form of Damietta, from Ancient Egyptian Tamiat through Coptic.
The Fifth Crusade took it after an eighteen-month siege in 1219.
It is Egypt’s furniture-making capital, with thousands of small workshops.
matruh: Marsa Matruh, "the harbour of Matruh" — marsa is an anchorage.
Its harbour was ancient Paraetonium, and Cleopatra is said to have swum in a cove nearby.
El Alamein, where the 1942 battle turned the desert war, is along this coast.
bur-said: Port Said in Arabic — bur is port, and Said was the viceroy who granted the canal concession.
Built in 1859 with the northern entrance of the Suez Canal.
The Anglo-French invasion of 1956 landed here, and the city’s resistance is a national story.
el-arish: Arabic for "the booth" or "the palm-frond shelter".
The largest town in Sinai and its administrative capital.
It sits on the ancient coast road between Egypt and Palestine, walked by armies in both directions for millennia.
el-mansura: "The victorious" — named for the defeat of the Fifth Crusade here in 1221.
Louis IX of France was captured in a house in this town in 1250, ending his crusade.
Its university has one of Egypt’s best-regarded medical faculties.
damanhur: From Ancient Egyptian Dmi-n-Hor, "the town of Horus" — a name over three thousand years old.
It was Hermopolis Parva to the Greeks.
It sits in the western Delta and is a centre of the cotton trade.
tanta: Of Ancient Egyptian origin, worn down through Coptic Tantathō.
Its mulid for al-Sayyid al-Badawi draws crowds comparable in size to the Hajj.
It is the largest town of the central Delta and a cotton-ginning centre.
zagazig: Of uncertain origin — possibly from a family name, or from an Arabic word for a mound.
Bubastis beside it was the cult city of Bastet, the cat goddess, whose festival Herodotus called the rowdiest in Egypt.
Ahmed Urabi, who led the 1879 revolt against foreign control, came from a village nearby.
shibin-el-kom: "Shibin of the mound" — kom is a mound of ancient debris, the standard word in Egyptian place names.
The capital of Monufia, the province that produced two Egyptian presidents.
Entirely surrounded by Delta farmland, some of the most intensively cultivated soil on earth.
benha: From Ancient Egyptian through Coptic Panaho.
Athribis beside it was an ancient capital, and a hoard of gold and silver was found there in 1924.
It is known across Egypt for its honey and its sweets.
el-faiyum: From Coptic phiom, "the lake" — itself from Ancient Egyptian pa-yom, the sea.
One of the oldest cities in Egypt, known to the Greeks as Crocodilopolis for the crocodile god worshipped there.
Its mummy portraits, painted on wood in the Roman period, are the most lifelike faces to survive from antiquity.
samalut: Of Coptic origin, from an older Egyptian settlement name.
It sits opposite Gebel el-Teir, a cliff-top monastery said to have sheltered the Holy Family.
The town is a sugar-cane and cotton centre on the west bank of the Nile.
el-minya: Amarna nearby was Akhenaten’s capital, built and abandoned within one reign for his one-god religion.
It is called the bride of Upper Egypt and has the largest Christian population share in the country.
mallawi: Of Coptic or older Egyptian origin.
Tuna el-Gebel nearby holds catacombs with millions of mummified ibises and baboons sacred to Thoth.
Its museum was looted and burned in 2013; many objects were later recovered.
hurghada: From an Arabic word for a local thorny plant, hurghad.
A fishing village until the 1980s, now the main Red Sea resort with hundreds of hotels.
Giftun island offshore is a protected area, and the reefs here are among the most heat-tolerant in the world.
girga: Named for a Coptic monastery of St George — Girga is George.
It was the capital of Upper Egypt under the Ottomans.
Abydos, the cult centre of Osiris and site of the king list that gave Egyptology its chronology, is in its district.
kom-ombo: "The mound of Ombos" — kom a mound, Ombos from Ancient Egyptian Nubt, "the golden".
Its temple is double, divided down the middle between the crocodile god Sobek and the falcon god Haroeris.
A wall there carves what appear to be surgical instruments, among the earliest medical illustrations known.
